insider_note: Splitting cos⁶x as cos⁴x·cos²x and pairing sin⁴x/cos⁴x with the leftover 1/cos²x works because the power of cosx underneath is more than the power of sinx on top by an even number (6 − 4 = 2). The ratio is then tanᵐx times an even power of secx, which always leaves a sec²x for dt. An even power of cosx on its own is not enough: sin³x/cos⁴x = tan³x·secx leaves no sec²x.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Rewrite as tan⁴x sec²x and substitute t = tanx
lines: Split the powers so that sec²x is left over

lines.text: to become the dt of a substitution:

lines: Put tanx = t ⇒ sec²x dx = dt
steps.why: Splitting the even power cos⁶x into cos⁴x (paired with sin⁴x to make tan⁴x) and a leftover cos²x (which becomes sec²x) leaves exactly a t=tanx substitution, since sec²x is tanx's own derivative.
common_mistakes: Splitting cos⁶x unevenly, e.g. as cos²x·cos⁴x paired the wrong way with sin⁴x, which does not leave a clean sec²x.
Trying t=sinx or t=cosx instead of t=tanx, neither of which matches the sec²x factor left over.
steps.memory_tip: Power of cosx below minus power of sinx above is even ⇒ tanᵐx times an even power of secx; take out sec²x dx = dt, and t = tanx.

steps.label: Integrate and back-substitute for the final answer
steps.why: ∫t⁴dt = t⁵/5 + c by the power rule, and substituting t=tanx back in gives the final answer as a fifth power of tanx over 5.
common_mistakes: Writing tan⁴x/4 instead of tan⁵x/5 — the power rule raises the power by one and divides by the new power.
Forgetting to substitute tanx back in for t.
steps.memory_tip: t⁴ integrates to t⁵/5 — the power goes up by one, and the new (higher) power is what you divide by.
